metadata.title: C172 JT-A Systems Trainer
metadata.studyNotice: Study concept only. Fuel-system wording is based on the provided Cessna 172 R&S TAE 125-02-114 POH supplement excerpt, but this trainer is not POH/AFM, checklist, maintenance, or operating guidance.
sourceNotes: Source used this pass: Supplement POH Cessna 172 R&S with TAE 125-02-114, Fuel System, pages 7-4 to 7-6, Issue 2 Revision 8, Nov. 2016.
Figure 7-3 labels include fuel tank right/left, fuel selector, reservoir tank, shut-off valve, electric pump, fuel filter module, fuel cooler, check valve, tank venting/indication items, and engine.
Exact aircraft procedures, limitations, annunciator wording, and maintenance detail must still be verified against the current approved documents for the specific aircraft.

systems.name: Electrical System
systems.summary: Buses, battery, alternator/generator logic, essential power paths, and annunciations.

systems.name: Fuel System
systems.summary: TAE 125-02-114 C172 fuel-system study model: original C172 tanks, selector, reservoir, shut-off valve, electric pump, filter module, engine-driven/high-pressure supply, rail injection, cooler, and return through the selector.

components.name: Fuel Tank Left
components.what: Stores usable fuel on the left side. The supplement states the installation uses the original Cessna 172 tanks.
components.failure: If the selected tank cannot supply usable fuel, the downstream system can be starved even if other components are healthy.
components.normal: Fuel available, level indication monitored, venting normal, and selected source available through the selector.
components.abnormal: Low fuel warning, unexpected imbalance, fuel temperature concern, contamination, or loss of feed from the selected side.

components.name: Fuel Tank Right
components.what: Stores usable fuel on the right side. The supplement states the installation uses the original Cessna 172 tanks.
components.failure: If the selected tank cannot supply usable fuel, the downstream system can be starved even if other components are healthy.
components.normal: Fuel available, level indication monitored, venting normal, and selected source available through the selector.
components.abnormal: Low fuel warning, unexpected imbalance, fuel temperature concern, contamination, or loss of feed from the selected side.

components.name: Tank Indications
components.what: Represents the fuel tank temperature indication, fuel tank level indication, and low fuel warning items shown in the fuel-system scheme.
components.failure: Incorrect or unavailable indications reduce the pilot's ability to monitor fuel quantity/temperature and low-fuel state.
components.normal: Tank level, fuel temperature, and low-fuel logic provide useful monitoring information.
components.abnormal: Disagreement, low fuel warning, fuel temperature outside limits, or missing indication.

components.name: Fuel Tank Venting Line
components.what: Represents tank venting shown in the fuel-system scheme. Venting allows the tanks to feed normally.
components.failure: A blocked vent can oppose normal fuel flow as fuel is drawn from the tank.
components.normal: Tank pressure equalization supports normal feed.
components.abnormal: Reduced feed, tank deformation risk in a general fuel-system sense, or unexplained fuel-flow difficulty.

components.name: Fuel Selector
components.what: Selects LEFT, RIGHT, or BOTH for feed. Surplus fuel returns through the selector to the pre-selected tank; if BOTH is selected, return fuel goes to both tanks.
components.failure: Incorrect selection, blockage, or selection mismatch can remove or limit the intended feed and return path.
components.normal: Selected tank path supplies the reservoir tank, and return flow is routed to the selected tank logic.
components.abnormal: Unexpected fuel imbalance, loss of feed, incorrect return path, or low-pressure symptoms.

components.name: Reservoir Tank
components.what: Fuel flows from the selector through a reservoir tank before the fuel shut-off valve.
components.failure: A leak, blockage, or venting problem here can interrupt the downstream supply path.
components.normal: Acts as the documented intermediate tank/collector in the feed path.
components.abnormal: Feed interruption, air/venting concerns, or downstream pressure loss.

components.name: Reservoir Vent / Check Valve
components.what: Represents the reservoir tank venting line and check valve shown in Figure 7-3.
components.failure: A venting or check-valve problem can affect reservoir behavior and fuel-system stability.
components.normal: Reservoir vent/check path supports the reservoir function.
components.abnormal: Unstable supply behavior or unexplained feed restriction in this study model.

components.name: Fuel Shut-off Valve
components.what: Fuel flows from the reservoir tank to the fuel shut-off valve before reaching the electric pump.
components.failure: A closed, blocked, or failed valve can stop fuel flow to the engine feed system.
components.normal: Open for normal operation so fuel can continue to the pump/filter side.
components.abnormal: Fuel starvation symptoms, low pressure, or engine power loss if the path is blocked.

components.name: Electric Pump
components.what: The supplement says the electrically driven fuel pump supports fuel flow to the filter module if required.
components.failure: Loss of electric-pump support reduces margin where electric pump assistance is required or expected.
components.normal: Available to support fuel flow to the filter module.
components.abnormal: Fuel pressure/flow concern, abnormal pump behavior, or reduced backup/support margin.

components.name: Fuel Filter Module
components.what: Filters fuel before engine feed. The supplement also states a temperature sensor in the filter module controls heat exchange between fuel feed and return.
components.failure: Restriction can reduce downstream flow. A temperature/heat-exchange control problem can affect fuel temperature management.
components.normal: Fuel passes through the filter module and heat exchange is controlled as designed.
components.abnormal: Reduced fuel flow/pressure, fuel temperature concern, or engine-running symptoms.

components.name: Engine-driven Feed Pump
components.what: After the filter module, the engine-driven feed pump supplies fuel toward the high-pressure pump.
components.failure: Failure can remove the engine-driven supply stage and degrade or stop fuel delivery to the high-pressure system.
components.normal: Provides engine-driven supply pressure while the engine is operating.
components.abnormal: Fuel pressure loss, reduced power, rough running, or engine stoppage risk.

components.name: High-pressure Pump
components.what: The supplement states the engine-driven feed pump and high-pressure pump supply the rail.
components.failure: Insufficient rail pressure can prevent correct injection and may cause power loss or engine shutdown.
components.normal: Supplies the rail with the pressure required for FADEC-regulated injection.
components.abnormal: Rail pressure abnormality, reduced power, rough running, or FADEC-related messages.

components.name: Rail
components.what: Receives supply from the engine-driven feed and high-pressure pumps, then supports cylinder injection.
components.failure: Pressure loss or rail-related faults can affect injection to the cylinders.
components.normal: Fuel is available for injection according to thrust lever position and FADEC regulation.
components.abnormal: Rail pressure fault, unstable power, roughness, or engine power loss.

components.name: Injectors / Cylinders
components.what: Fuel is injected into the cylinders depending upon thrust lever position and FADEC regulation.
components.failure: Injection faults can affect combustion, smoothness, and power.
components.normal: FADEC-regulated injection delivers fuel to the cylinders.
components.abnormal: Rough running, reduced power, abnormal engine parameters, or FADEC fault cues.

components.name: Engine
components.what: Represents the engine receiving injected fuel and producing power under FADEC/single-lever style management.
components.failure: Fuel starvation, injection faults, or rail pressure faults can reduce power or stop the engine.
components.normal: Stable operation for the selected thrust lever command.
components.abnormal: Power loss, roughness, abnormal engine indications, or engine alerts.

components.name: Fuel Cooler
components.what: Surplus fuel flows to the fuel cooler. The supplement states the fuel cooler reduces fuel temperature in the return line.
components.failure: Reduced cooling can increase return-fuel temperature and reduce thermal margin.
components.normal: Return fuel is cooled before routing back through the selector.
components.abnormal: Fuel temperature concern, especially where operating limits or high OAT cooling configuration matter.

components.name: Cooler Air Inlet / Baffle
components.what: The supplement states the fuel cooler receives cooling air through an inlet in the heating-radiator air duct. The inlet is closed with a baffle that must be removed at OAT above 20 degrees C / 68 degrees F.
components.failure: Incorrect baffle configuration can reduce fuel-cooler effectiveness in high outside air temperatures.
components.normal: Cooling-air configuration matches the approved operating guidance.
components.abnormal: Fuel temperature rise or reduced cooling margin in warm conditions.

scenarios.name: Normal Operation
scenarios.description: Fuel flows from the selected tank path through the selector, reservoir tank, shut-off valve, electric pump, filter module, engine-driven feed pump, high-pressure pump, rail, and injectors. Surplus fuel flows to the cooler and then back through the selector.
scenarios.consequence: Study note: normal feed and return are shown, including BOTH-style return to both tanks. Exact aircraft indications and operating procedures remain POH/AFM items.

scenarios.name: Electric Fuel Pump OFF
scenarios.description: The electrically driven pump is not supporting flow. The documented role is support to the filter module if required.
scenarios.consequence: Study note: less electric-pump support to the filter module. Monitor fuel and engine indications and use approved procedures.

scenarios.name: Fuel Filter Restricted
scenarios.description: The filter module is restricted, reducing downstream flow to the engine-driven feed pump and high-pressure/rail side.
scenarios.consequence: Study note: restriction at the filter module can reduce downstream supply and affect rail pressure, injection, and power.

scenarios.name: Tank Selected LEFT
scenarios.description: LEFT is selected. Feed is from the left tank, and surplus return is routed through the selector back into the pre-selected left tank.
scenarios.consequence: Study note: left feed and left return are active; right feed/return are inactive. Think source management, temperature, and imbalance.

scenarios.name: Tank Selected RIGHT
scenarios.description: RIGHT is selected. Feed is from the right tank, and surplus return is routed through the selector back into the pre-selected right tank.
scenarios.consequence: Study note: right feed and right return are active; left feed/return are inactive. Think source management, temperature, and imbalance.

scenarios.name: Engine Driven Pump Failure
scenarios.description: The engine-driven feed pump has failed, interrupting the documented supply path to the high-pressure pump and rail.
scenarios.consequence: Study note: loss of the engine-driven feed pump threatens supply to the high-pressure pump, rail, and injectors. This trainer does not prescribe procedures.

faults.name: Fail Electric Fuel Pump
faults.pilotIndication: Possible fuel pressure/flow concern where electric pump support is required or expected.
faults.risk: Reduced support to the filter module and downstream feed system.
faults.response: Study note: monitor fuel and engine indications and use approved aircraft procedures.

faults.name: Restrict Fuel Filter
faults.pilotIndication: Possible reduced fuel flow/pressure, rail pressure issue, rough running, or reduced power in a final aircraft-specific indication model.
faults.risk: Downstream starvation and inability to maintain commanded rail pressure.
faults.response: Study note: identify restriction symptoms, monitor engine indications, and use approved abnormal guidance.

faults.name: Fail Engine Driven Pump
faults.pilotIndication: Likely fuel pressure/rail supply or engine power abnormality in this study model.
faults.risk: High-pressure pump and rail may not receive adequate supply, with possible power loss.
faults.response: Study note: maintain aircraft control, diagnose with indications, and follow approved procedures.

faults.name: Block Return Line
faults.pilotIndication: Possible fuel temperature or return-flow abnormality if modeled by exact aircraft indications.
faults.risk: Surplus fuel return and fuel-temperature management may be compromised.
faults.response: Study note: monitor fuel temperature/engine indications and use approved aircraft guidance.

faults.name: Select Left Tank Only
faults.pilotIndication: Feed and return are focused on the selected left tank in this study model.
faults.risk: Fuel imbalance, selected-source depletion, or temperature concentration in the tank in use.
faults.response: Study note: verify source selection and manage fuel according to approved procedures.

faults.name: Select Right Tank Only
faults.pilotIndication: Feed and return are focused on the selected right tank in this study model.
faults.risk: Fuel imbalance, selected-source depletion, or temperature concentration in the tank in use.
faults.response: Study note: verify source selection and manage fuel according to approved procedures.

memoryMode.instructions: Click the tiles in the documented feed order. Either tank can count as the selected tank. The return/cooler path is tested through the diagram and oral prompts rather than the core feed sequence.

oralQuestions.prompt: Explain the documented feed path from tank to cylinder injection.
oralQuestions.modelAnswer: Study answer: fuel flows from the selected tank through the fuel selector, reservoir tank, fuel shut-off valve, electric pump, and fuel filter module. From there, the engine-driven feed pump and high-pressure pump supply the rail, and fuel is injected into the cylinders according to thrust lever position and FADEC regulation.

oralQuestions.prompt: Explain the surplus fuel return path and what happens with BOTH selected.
oralQuestions.modelAnswer: Study answer: surplus fuel flows to the fuel cooler, then through the fuel selector back into the pre-selected tank. If BOTH is selected, the return goes to both tanks.

oralQuestions.prompt: What is special about the fuel filter module in this system?
oralQuestions.modelAnswer: Study answer: it is not just a filter in the study model. The supplement says a temperature sensor in the filter module controls heat exchange between the fuel feed and return.

oralQuestions.prompt: Explain what happens if the electric pump is unavailable.
oralQuestions.modelAnswer: Study answer: the electric pump supports fuel flow to the filter module if required. If unavailable, the system has less support margin, and the pilot should monitor fuel/engine indications and use approved aircraft procedures.

oralQuestions.prompt: Why does fuel temperature matter in this diesel/Jet-A installation?
oralQuestions.modelAnswer: Study answer: the supplement notes low-temperature paraffin formation concerns for diesel fuel and requires fuel-temperature limits to be monitored. Return fuel also helps warm the tank in use, while the fuel cooler reduces return-line temperature.

oralQuestions.prompt: What does the supplement say about the fuel cooler air inlet baffle?
oralQuestions.modelAnswer: Study answer: the fuel cooler receives cooling air through an inlet in the heating-radiator air duct. The inlet is closed with a baffle, which must be removed at OAT above 20 degrees C / 68 degrees F according to the supplement. Treat this as a study note, not an operating instruction.
